doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Early records and hearing Dizzy Gillespie at Georgetown
summary: Childhood 78s from Art Hodes, an Art Tatum trio LP, then Dizzy's playing at a festival hooked him on modern jazz.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well no. I had Art Hodes’ records when I was five years old. My older brother and Bob Hodes, Art’s son, were in first grade together in West Hempstead Long Island. We lived there for a very brief period of time when I was like three, four and five. So my father and Art Hodes, and my mother and Art and Thelma Hodes they all became friends. And so I had these 78s. I have a few of them left. “Way Down Yonder in New Orleans” is on one side and a tune called “Save It Pretty Mama” is on the other side. I can’t believe they got it printed back then you know. It’s not a vocal. But I didn’t pay much attention to it until, oh I had some Hackett records believe it or not. And I had an Art Tatum trio record which my mother bought for me to give to my step-grandfather for Christmas. And about two days later he gave it back to me.
Yeah. It was a record with Slam Stewart and Everett Barksdale. And it was a ten inch LP and I had it stolen in the 70s when I had a whole footlocker — my prize possessions gone.

Oh yeah, yeah sure. And so but I don’t know, when I was in high school, that’s when I really got the bug. And a buddy of mine took me to hear Dizzy Gillespie one night, he was adjudicating a festival at Georgetown University. The second place band was a six piece bebop band led by Paul Winter.

Yeah. Like a Art Blakey style band. And they came in second. And then Dizzy played. And I’d never heard Dizzy on record, and being a trumpet player, I mean I am sure that my hair literally stood on end when he started playing for the first time. And I of course immediately raced out and bought everything. And then it was Miles and all the saxophone players and so the music I was listening to when I entered as a listener were the people that were hot at the time. Miles, Cannonball, Wes Montgomery, Wynton Kelly, Wayne Shorter, those kind of people. I had to go back and find out about Louis. To me Louis meant nothing to me at the time. It was just an old guy.
Yeah. I guess that’s usually the way it happens.

Yeah. I’m sure it is. But once I got interested in the earlier music then I really went back and took a good long hard look at it and got emotionally involved in it, and then it became part of me just like the music of the 60s, you know, the Wes Montgomery things that I still get out and listen to all that stuff. I love that music period.
